region: Carnation Creek, west coast of Vancouver Island, BC
quote: Sub-model 2 predicts the median emergence date of the fry from the Celsius thermal summations for February and March
note: Base not stated (a Celsius thermal summation). Window: February-March. Eq. 14 as printed: JDemerge (Julian) = -0.272 * CTSfebmar + 190.2 (r=0.892, n=16, P<0.001). Same page: 'Emergence timing is strongly correlated with late winter stream temperatures (Holtby 1988c; Scrivener and Andersen 1984).' The coho model then predicts fall fingerling fork length from emergence date and summer density (eq. 17, p. 70: FLfall = -0.254 * JDemerge, a density term 0.0005 * gmDensity whose sign the text layer does not show, + 91.7; r=0.912, n=16, P<0.001) and winter survival from fall fork length (eq. 18, p. 70, its own row). The fall-size equation has no summer temperature term, so temperature enters the coho model through emergence timing (p. 70: summer growth rates not affected by increased summer temperatures, its own row). No threshold.

region: Carnation Creek, west coast of Vancouver Island, BC
quote: Most of the variability in winter survival was associated with changes in fish size going into the winter.
note: Eq. 18 (sub-model 6, p. 70) as printed: Pwinter survival = -1.188 + 0.0232 * FLfall + 0.288 * HQIw (r=0.897, n=17, P<0.001); the text layer renders the first '+' as '-I-'. Pwinter survival is the probability that sub-yearling fingerlings survive the winter; FLfall is their mean fork length (mm) in the fall of their first year (sub-model 5); HQIw is a 0-1 winter habitat-quality index from biologists' ratings, which turned on large pools and stable large organic debris (p. 64). Same paragraph: 'Winter survivals were greatest when HQIw signified large pool and debris volumes.' No threshold length is printed. Yearling (second-winter) survival and the asymptote are a separate row (p. 71). Hartman & Scrivener 1990 (p. 88, Fig. 72) prints the single-variable fit of survival on autumn fork length.

region: Carnation Creek, west coast of Vancouver Island, BC
quote: Interestingly the estimated average survival of yearlings, 0.645, is similar to the survivals of the largest of the sub-yearlings, suggesting that over-winter survival is an asymptotic function of size
note: The sentence ends '(Holtby 1988b)'. The sentence before it: 'Unlike the sub-yearlings, the over-winter survival of the yearlings was not correlated with the size at which they entered the winter' (their second winter). 0.645 is a survival proportion, not a length; no length at which survival levels off is printed. The first-winter regression on fall fork length is eq. 18 (p. 70, its own row).

region: Carnation Creek, west coast of Vancouver Island, BC
quote: when averaged over all of the study sections, summer growth rates were not affected by logging, and in particular, were not affected by increased summer stream temperatures
note: Sub-yearling coho, first summer. The sentence ends '(Holtby 1988c)' (Can. J. Fish. Aquat. Sci. 45) and begins 'Although summer growth rates did increase in some stream reaches immediately after logging (Scrivener and Andersen 1984)'. Counter-evidence to a summer-temperature effect on first-summer growth rate; the coho model takes temperature through emergence timing (eq. 14, p. 69, its own row). Contrast Hartman & Scrivener 1990 p. 83: summer thermal summation positively correlated with autumn fry fork length and weight (Holtby 1988) - a size, where this is a growth rate.

region: Carnation Creek, west coast of Vancouver Island, BC
quote: The over-winter survival of yearling coho, i.e. from eggs layed 12-14 mo earlier, was dependent on their size in autumn. Survival during the first winter was positively correlated with size, both length (Fig. 72)
note: Fig. 72 (p. 88) prints y = 0.0212x - 0.837, r = 0.91, p < 0.001 (text layer 'y0.0212x-0.837'): survival rate during the subsequent winter against fork length (mm) of age 0+ coho in the autumn, 1970 to 1987; the x axis runs 45 to 75 mm. The sentence goes on: 'and. weight (r = 0.88, n = 14, P < 0.001 ; Holtby 1988)'. Same page: Holtby (1988) suggested the positive relation of stream temperature to first-winter survival 'might simply reflect a shorter period of egg incubation (leading to larger size in autumn, Fig. 68 ; and consequently a higher over-winter survival)'. p. 106 repeats that larger autumn fry 'had higher over winter survival (Fig. 72)'. No threshold length is printed. Holtby & Scrivener 1989 (p. 70) give the two-variable model with winter habitat quality.

region: Carnation Creek, west coast of Vancouver Island, BC
quote: Day-of-the-year of 50 % emergence was also correlated with stream temperature during egg incubation, e.g., thermal summation of daily means of stream temperature
cited_source: Hartman et al. 1984; Scrivener and Andersen 1984
note: Base not stated (a summation of daily mean stream temperatures). Window: egg incubation, not otherwise defined on this page. No coefficient printed. The sentence before: 'Day-of-the-year when 50 % of the fry had emerged was strongly correlated with their size in autumn (r = -0.96, n = 16, P < .001)'; the sentence after: 'Warmer winters led to earlier emergence and a longer growing season.' p. 88: 'Stream temperature influenced fish size mainly by shortening the egg incubation period ; thus lengthening the growth period during their first summer.' Holtby & Scrivener 1989 (p. 69, eq. 14) print the February-March regression.

region: Carnation Creek, west coast of Vancouver Island, BC
quote: stream temperature during the summer, thermal summation of mean daily temperatures at B-weir, was positively correlated with fry FL and weight in the autumn
note: Base not stated (a summation of mean daily temperatures). Window: 'during the summer', not otherwise defined on this page. No coefficient printed. Age 0+ coho. Hartman & Scrivener cite three Holtby 1988 items; which one carries this is not stated. On the same page the duration of the summer growth period, 'extended by earlier emergence of fry, had the greatest positive effect on fry FL and weight in the autumn'. p. 84: the growth rate of age 1+ coho was negatively correlated with summer thermal summation, 'in contrast with age 0+ coho (Holtby 1988)'. Contrast Holtby & Scrivener 1989 p. 70: summer growth rates not affected by increased summer temperatures (its own row).

region: Mid-Fraser River tributaries (Thompson and Chilcotin systems), BC
quote: Smolt ages were estimated based on the mean annual number of degree days > 7o C for each system coupled with a requirement of 450 such days prior to smoltification.
note: Base 7 C ('> 7o C': the text layer renders the degree sign as 'o'). Window: accumulated before smoltification, over however many years that takes; the start is not stated. Smolt age was estimated from each system's mean annual degree-days above 7 C together with this requirement. As printed, '450 such days' follows 'degree days > 7o C', so it is read as 450 degree-days above 7 C. No source is cited for the rule. A smolting requirement for steelhead parr, not a first-winter survival threshold. Same page: the smolt ages estimated this way are the data for the fit of mean smolt age on age 1+ parr fork length (SMAGE = 587.203 * FL1 ^ -1.14116, r2 = 0.996, eight systems), and fry-to-smolt survival falls with smolt age (equations modified from Symons 1979).

region: Beaver, Gold and Moore creeks, West Fork Smith River (Umpqua basin), Oregon
quote: Among individual coho salmon tagged within the tributaries, probability of survival was positively associated with FL, condition factor, and reach location at the time of tagging in the fall
note: Logistic regression of apparent overwinter survival (Table 7, p. 1690): fork length chi-square 5.64, df 1, P = 0.018; condition factor 5.28, P = 0.022; reach of origin 25.13, P < 0.001; the model explains 8.7 % of deviance (adjusted 7.6 %). One cohort, tagged in three periods between August 19 and November 14, 2002 (p. 1685); only fish of 60 mm FL or larger were PIT-tagged. 'Apparent' survival includes emigration from the study area. The 90 mm statement in the next sentence is its own row. Abstract (p. 1681): 'Fall body size of juvenile coho salmon was a good predictor of smolt size and survival'.

region: Beaver, Gold and Moore creeks, West Fork Smith River (Umpqua basin), Oregon
quote: Survival was highest for coho salmon that were larger than 90 mm at the time of tagging (Figure 5)
note: Fork length at fall tagging (August to November 2002). Figure 5 (p. 1691) plots apparent overwinter survival by fork-length class (60-69, 70-79, 80-89, >90 mm) for each of the three tributaries: 90 mm is the lower edge of the top class, not a fitted threshold, and fish under 60 mm were not tagged. The logistic model explains 8.7 % of deviance (Table 7; its own row). One cohort. Ebersole et al. 2009 (p. 569) restate this result as survival that 'increased markedly above 80 mm' and use 80 mm as their threshold (its own row).

region: West Fork Smith River (Umpqua basin), southwestern Oregon
quote: We used 80 mm as the threshold for fall parr length (% suitable FL, FLs), based upon previously reported ... overwinter survival of juvenile coho salmon that increased markedly above 80 mm (Ebersole et al. 2006)
note: A hypothesized critical length: the survival models took the percent of a reach's tagged fall parr above 80 mm fork length (FLs). Result (p. 571): FLs was positively associated with survival, 'as predicted', but was in only 51 % of the top models, had low relative importance (0.64) and a CI that included zero; the abstract calls fall fork length 'relatively uninformative' (its own row). Ebersole et al. 2006 (p. 1690) itself states survival was highest above 90 mm. The quote skips the OCR word 'sizedependent'.

region: West Fork Smith River (Umpqua basin), southwestern Oregon
quote: Indices of individual fish condition, including fall parr fork length, condition factor, and parasite infestation rates, were also relatively uninformative in coho salmon overwinter survival models.
note: Counter-evidence. Fish tagged between August 15 and October 31 in 2003, 2004 and 2005 (p. 567); survival was summarized by reach, and contributing basin area explained most of its spatial variation (abstract). p. 571: the fall-length predictor (percent above 80 mm, its own row) had relative importance 0.64 and a CI including zero. p. 574: results on fall size 'appear to be dependent upon winter severity', and if relative size (Zabel and Achord 2004) matters more, absolute size metrics 'might fail to capture' it. p. 575: high winter growth in intermittent streams let relatively small parr 'catch up' in growth and emigrate larger than fall size predicts.

region: West Fork Smith River (Umpqua basin), southwestern Oregon
quote: The size of a smolt was positively related to cumulative temperature units accrued from January 1 to the day of capture at the smolt trap
note: Base 0 C: 'cumulative degree-days (above 0 C; Neuheimer and Taggart 2007)' (p. 568). Window: January 1, during the first winter, to the date of capture at the smolt trap (early February to early June). The median parameter estimate is 0.06, 'indicating that an increase of 100 cumulative temperature units before capture at the smolt trap conferred a 6-mm increase in smolt length' (p. 572). The authors say the estimate 'primarily indexes date of emigration' (p. 568). Smolt length, not survival, and not the first summer; smolt length was primarily a function of fall fork length (abstract).

quote: Fish in larger size-classes showed a higher survival rate than smaller fish in 1990–1991
note: The sentence goes on: '(chi2 = 15.40, p < 0.01) but not in 1991-1992 (chi2 = 0.98, p = 0.91; Fig. 2)'. Length classes (mm) in early October (<60, 60-69, 70-79, 80-89, >89 mm; Fig. 2, p. 1558), fish below William Symington Lake. Table 1 (p. 1558): mean length of survivors 75.7 +/- 7.8 mm against nonsurvivors 73.6 +/- 7.4 mm in 1990-1991 (p < 0.01), 76.5 +/- 8.1 against 76.0 +/- 7.8 mm in 1991-1992. p. 1560: 'for a given size-class, survival differed between years (Fig. 2), indicating that factors other than habitat conditions and fish size affected mortality'; the 1990 group's maximum daily winter flow was almost twice the 1991 group's. Survival is recovery of marked smolts at the weir, so fish leaving before or after the smolt run count as mortalities (p. 1557). No threshold length.

quote: However, fish tagged above William Symington Lake were smaller in the fall but larger as smolts and had higher survival rates than those tagged below the lake.
note: Counter-evidence to an absolute fall-length threshold. Table 2 (p. 1558): fall length 69.8 +/- 9.3 mm for fish tagged above the lake against 77.3 +/- 7.2 mm below it; survival 56.7 against 44.1 % in 1991 (p. 1557). The authors say such rapid growth 'would be consistent with pond or lake residence', though the fish might also have overwintered in wetlands above the lake (p. 1559).
